1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5.name: Bishop's Opening: Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5.background: Black's symmetrical reply, also called the Boi Variation, and after 2...Nf6 and 2...Nc6 the next most common answer to 2.Bc4.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3.name: Bishop's Opening: Philidor Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3.strategy: Prepares d4, which would give White a broad pawn centre with tempo on the bishop. The price is that the pawn takes the c3 square from the queen's knight and White is slow to develop, so the game stays quiet and strategic unless Black reacts to the threatened centre at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4.name: Bishop's Opening: McDonnell Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to drag the bishop off its diagonal: if Black takes, c3 hits it with tempo and White gets a broad pawn centre for the pawn. It is the Evans Gambit idea played before the king's knight is out, so White gambles on time and the centre, not on material.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.d4.name: Bishop's Opening: Lewis Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.d4.strategy: Challenges the bishop and the centre at once by offering the d-pawn. Black can take it with the e-pawn or the bishop, because the bishop guards d4 and the queen cannot recapture there, so White has to play for open lines and development against an extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2.name: Bishop's Opening: Lopez Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2.strategy: Defends e4 and f2 with the queen, but it takes the e2 square from the bishop and does nothing against Black's symmetrical set-up, so Black develops without difficulty. A quiet, harmless move.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.f4.name: Bishop's Opening: Stein Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.f4.strategy: Strikes at e5 as in the King's Gambit, but the bishop on c5 makes it loose: the f-pawn no longer shields the king's diagonal and the bishop eyes the knight on g1. The game stays roughly level, yet White opens lines before developing a piece, and Black can answer in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight attacks e5 and prepares castling, and White keeps every plan open, from a slow build-up to a central strike. Black has to defend the pawn at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4.strategy: Accepts the gambit: Black wins a pawn, but the bishop will be hit again by c3 and spend time on the move. The extra pawn is kept by developing calmly and not letting White's centre and open lines grow unchallenged.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bb6.strategy: Declines the pawn and keeps the bishop on its diagonal against f2, out of reach of c3. White has advanced a wing pawn for nothing so far, and Black avoids the gambit's open play for a calm game.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bd6.strategy: Declines the pawn by retreating to guard e5, but the bishop leaves its active diagonal and blocks the d-pawn, so Black's development becomes awkward. White keeps the advanced b-pawn and gets time to build the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4 4.c3.name: Bishop's Opening: McDonnell Gambit, La Bourdonnais-Denker Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4 4.c3.strategy: Hits the bishop at once and prepares a broad pawn centre, so White's pieces come out with tempo while the bishop has to move again. This is the usual way to claim compensation for the pawn: the centre and the open lines are the return on it.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4 4.f4.name: Bishop's Opening: McDonnell Gambit, McDonnell Double Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4 4.f4.strategy: Offers a second pawn to pull Black's e-pawn out of the centre and open the f-file. It is a gamble too far: if Black takes, White is two pawns down, and the centre and lead in development it can build do not pay for both.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4 4.Nf3.strategy: Attacks the undefended e5 pawn and develops with tempo. White can still hit the bishop with c3 and reach the usual gambit positions, but Black gets extra choices in how to defend and where to put the bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4 4.f4 exf4.strategy: Takes the second pawn and leaves White without a pawn in the centre but the e-pawn. Black is two pawns up and has to finish development before White's pieces and centre arrive; every tempo counts, and a calm, solid setup is Black's best chance to keep the material.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4 4.f4 d6.strategy: Declines the second pawn and keeps the first, freeing the c8-bishop and holding the centre. But it passes up the second pawn for a quiet set-up: White hits the bishop with c3 and develops with tempo, and Black is left only slightly better.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4 4.f4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a threat to e4 but leaves the offered pawn alone. White can open the centre or hit the bishop with c3, and Black, though still a pawn up, gives back much of the edge that taking the second pawn would keep.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.b4 Bxb4 4.f4 exf4 5..strategy: Develops with a purpose: the knight covers h4, so Black's queen cannot check there for free. It also prepares a central strike and castling, which is how White hopes to turn the lead in development into compensation for two pawns.
Attacks the bishop but ignores the queen check on h4: Black plays ...Qh4+ and White must give up castling or let the g-pawn fall. Black keeps both extra pawns and the initiative.

Gains space and takes f6 from Black's knight, but leaves h4 unguarded. The check on h4 forces White to give up castling or open the king's cover, and Black keeps both pawns with the better development.

Retreats the bishop to safety before c3 hits it and keeps both pawns. But it costs a move while White is ahead in development: White castles and builds the centre with tempo, and much of Black's advantage is gone.

Develops with a threat to e4 and keeps both extra pawns. The bishop on b4 may be hit by c3, but Black's pieces come out quickly and the king can castle soon. White has to show that its lead in development is worth two pawns.

Controls e5 and frees the c8-bishop, a calm way to develop. But it costs a move while White is ahead in development: c3 hits the bishop on b4 with tempo, and White builds the centre while the two extra pawns do little.

Builds the central pawn the gambit was played for and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal, so the f4 pawn is attacked at once. A respected plan, but it hurries: Black can answer by developing and keep both extra pawns while White's attack has yet to arrive.

Castles first: the king is safe and the rook comes to the f-file, so the central strike can wait until the pieces are ready. Black gets a move to consolidate, but White's lead in development remains, and holding both extra pawns is no easy task.
Aims the bishop at g7 along the long diagonal and supports a later e5. Black has to deal with the threat to the g7 pawn, but can do so while developing, and White still has not taken the centre.

Checks at once and forces White to answer, but nothing is won: after g3 the game is level, and the chance to keep both extra pawns with a calm developing move has been spent. Black's king is still in the middle.

Develops with a threat to e4 and keeps the bishop at home to guard the kingside, so Black stays two pawns up. White's centre and lead in development give real play, but Black can castle and meet the pressure with pieces.

Holds e5 and frees the c8-bishop, a calm way to develop. But the d-pawn has opened the c1-bishop's diagonal and the f4 pawn is attacked at once, so Black probably gives one pawn back to complete development.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4 at once, and lets White build the pawn centre it wants. Black does not stop the centre but counts on hitting it with pieces and a well-timed central break, which leads to the main line of this variation and to lively open play.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5.name: Bishop's Opening: Lewis Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5.background: Named for the English player and author William Lewis (1787–1870), who published analysis of the line in 1834.
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5.strategy: Meets the threatened centre by striking in the centre first: the pawn hits the bishop on c4 and opens lines for Black's pieces. If White takes the pawn, Black plays for quick development and activity instead of material, so this is the sharp, energetic answer.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Qg5.name: Bishop's Opening: del Rio Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Qg5.strategy: Brings the queen out early to hit g2. It is sound: if White strikes with d4, Black takes on g2 and the queens come off into an even game. But the raid spends time while the other pieces stay at home, so Black has to know what to do after White's centre strike.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.Bxd5.strategy: Takes the offered pawn with the bishop, which is guarded on d5 by the e-pawn, and avoids the tactic that punishes exd5. White is a pawn up, and Black has to prove that quick development makes up for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.exd5.strategy: Takes the pawn with the pawn, but the bishop on c4 is left loose: Black plays ...Bxf2+, and after Kxf2 Qh4+ the queen wins the bishop back, leaving material level and White's king stranded in the open.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.Bb5+.strategy: Checks first, but Black blocks with ...c6, which attacks the bishop again, and after the retreat ...dxe4 wins the e-pawn. White has lost time and a pawn with nothing to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.Bxd5 Nf6.name: Bishop's Opening: Lewis Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.Bxd5 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the bishop on d5 and the e4 pawn in one move, with a developing move. Black pays a pawn for tempo and lines: White has to resolve the tension in the centre before Black's pieces become too active.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.Bxd5 c6.strategy: Kicks the bishop with a pawn, but it costs time and takes the c6 square from the knight. The bishop simply retreats to b3, still on its diagonal against f7, and White keeps the extra pawn with a free hand in the centre while Black has nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.Bxd5 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight but ignores the threat to the centre: White plays d4 at once, hitting the bishop on c5 and the e5 pawn, and usually wins a second pawn. Black's lead in development does not make up for two pawns.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.Bxd5 Nf6 5.d.name: Bishop's Opening: Lewis Countergambit, Walker Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.Bxd5 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Counterattacks in the centre: the pawn hits the bishop on c5 and the e5 pawn at once, and the pawn on c3 supports it. The bishop on d5 stays exposed to Black's queen and knight, so the position is a sharp open fight over White's extra pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 d5 4.Bxd5 Nf6 5.B.strategy: Retreats the attacked bishop and keeps it on the diagonal against f7. Black takes e4 with the knight at once, winning the pawn back with an active piece that eyes f2 together with the bishop, so the game is about level.
Returns the bishop to where it started, keeping f7 under pressure. Black wins e4 back with the knight, and the bishop on c4 can be attacked again by a pawn, so White has spent time to end up level.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Plays the move that 3.c3 prepared: the pawn attacks the bishop and e5 and, backed by the pawn on c3, forms a broad centre. White claims space and the initiative, and Black has to act against the centre at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Solid: the pawn defends e4 and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal, and the centre pawns stay compact. White gives up the immediate central break for a slower, manoeuvring game in which neither side has an early target.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.Qe2.strategy: Protects e4 against the knight and keeps the centre pawn options open. But the queen takes the e2 square from the king's knight and does not claim the centre, so Black develops freely and the game is level.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Takes the pawn to break up the centre and keeps the e4 pawn under attack by the knight. The pawn has no defender, so White has to deal with that at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Bb6.strategy: Steps away from the pawn but gives up e5: the capture wins a pawn, and taking on e4 with the knight runs into the queen going to d5, which attacks the knight and threatens mate on f7.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 Nxe4.strategy: Grabs the pawn, but the d-pawn simply takes the bishop on c5. Black gets two pawns for the bishop, and the knight and the open centre do not make up for a whole piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5.e.strategy: Saves the attacked e4 pawn by advancing it with tempo on the knight, which cannot stay on f6. White gives up the pawn on d4 for a lead in space and initiative, and the game becomes a sharp fight where tactics decide.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5.c.strategy: Retakes with the pawn, hitting the bishop and restoring a pawn in the centre. The e4 pawn is loose to the knight, so after Black's check White must choose between defending it and playing for development in return; the game is open and tactical.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5.Q.strategy: Hangs the queen: the bishop on c5 takes it on d4, and after the recapture White has given a queen for a bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.c3 Nf6 4.d4 exd4 5.e.strategy: The counter-strike: instead of saving the knight, Black hits the bishop on c4 with a pawn. Both sides have a piece attacked, and Black accepts a trade of knight for bishop in return for central pawns and open lines.

Retreats the attacked knight all the way home, which undoes Black's development. White retakes on d4 with the pawn and has the centre and the lead in development; Black avoids the sharp play but gives up the initiative.
Hangs the knight: the bishop takes it, and Black's queen cannot recapture because the pawn on d7 blocks the d-file.

Takes the knight instead of saving the bishop, but Black takes the bishop on c4 in return and comes out a pawn up with the better position. The pawn on f6 gives White some play against g7, yet no attack that pays for the pawn.

Steps out of the pawn's attack with check, so the threat to the knight on f6 stays. Black must answer the check first, but the bishop can be traded off and the game stays level, with an open centre and chances for both.

A quiet retreat that keeps the bishop on the diagonal against f7 and out of the pawn's reach. The knight escapes with tempo to e4, where it attacks the c3 pawn, so the game stays level: White has the centre, Black the activity.

Takes the bishop with the pawn, so each side has lost a minor piece. Black has pawns on c4 and d4 and an active bishop on c5, but the pawn on f6 and the loose bishop are targets, so White's queen has real attacking chances.
Wrecks the pawn cover of Black's own king and does not solve the problem of the bishop on c5, which a pawn capture on d4 attacks again. Black ends up a pawn down in a damaged position.
Recaptures and forgets the bishop on c4: it simply takes the pawn on d5 with gain, leaving White a whole piece up. The queen's eye on f2 only makes tricks, not enough compensation.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6.strategy: Develops and defends e5 in one move, the solid reply to the quiet queen move. Black keeps the symmetrical structure and stays flexible, with no weaknesses and an easy game, while White's queen has still to find a useful task.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4, so the queen on e2 has to do the defending. Black gets a more active game than with the quiet defence of e5, and the queen is tied to the defence of the pawn on e4 for now.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 d6.strategy: Holds e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop: solid and free of weaknesses. It develops no piece, so Black gives White a free hand to organise the position, but nothing is lost.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.c3.strategy: Prepares a pawn centre with the queen guarding e4 and f2, so Black's bishop pressure on f2 is covered. White plays for a slow build-up in the centre; the cost is that the c3 pawn takes the square from the queen's knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks e5, which the knight on c6 holds. The queen on e2 already guards e4 and f2, so White can finish development in peace. The price is that no pawn centre is prepared, so the game stays level and manoeuvring.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.d3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn, which frees the queen from guarding it, and opens the c1-bishop. It is solid but slow: White gives up the central break for now, and Black develops freely and claims space.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.c3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4 again, asking the queen to keep defending it. Black completes the natural development of the minor pieces and is ready to castle, with a solid game and no weaknesses to worry about.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.c3 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn and opens the c8-bishop, a solid answer to a pawn centre. Black accepts a slightly passive set-up and must be ready to meet White's d4, which hits the bishop and the e5 pawn together, with an exchange in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.c3 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5 and f7 with the queen, but commits the queen early and puts it on the e-file facing White's. White can open the centre with d4, hitting the bishop and the e5 pawn together, and Black ends up with a passive game.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.c3 Nf6 5.f.name: Bishop's Opening: Lopez Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.c3 Nf6 5.f.strategy: Tries a gambit break against e5, but it loosens the king's side while the king is still on e1 and the bishop on c5 aims at g1. Black simply castles and, after the trade on e5, wins the e4 pawn with a lead in activity. White gets nothing for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.c3 Nf6 5.N.strategy: Develops and attacks e5, which the knight on c6 holds, so the move builds the kingside rather than forcing anything. The queen on e2 guards e4, so ...Nxe4 simply loses a piece to Qxe4. White heads for a slow build-up behind a solid pawn centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nc6 4.c3 Nf6 5.d.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn and gives the c1-bishop its diagonal. It is solid and flexible but slow: with the d-pawn on d3 White gives up the quick central break for a steady build-up, and Black has time to equalise.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nf6 4.f4.name: Bishop's Opening: Lopez Variation, Lopez Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nf6 4.f4.strategy: Tries a gambit break against e5, but with the f-pawn gone the king's side is open and the bishop on c5 aims at the knight on g1. Black strikes in the centre with ...d5, hitting the bishop and the e4 pawn, and White, with the king in the middle, has to defend.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nf6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks the undefended e5 pawn, so Black has to spend a move on it. The queen on e2 guards e4, which makes ...Nxe4 a blunder: Qxe4 wins the knight. White keeps the f-pawn at home and develops without weakening the king's side.

1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Bc5 3.Qe2 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Supports e4 with a pawn so the queen is free, and opens the c1-bishop. It is a solid, flexible set-up, but the d-pawn is no longer free to strike in the centre, so White settles for a steady build-up rather than the initiative.
